report.source_text: He presented for the third time the next day as a primary care referral due to urinary retention. 1300 mL of urine was seen on bladder scan and he was successfully catheterised. At this time normal power and sensation in his lower limbs were noted and there was normal anal tone on rectal examination. After an assessment by urology it was thought the retention was secondary to constipation, having started codeine recently. Bowels had last opened 3 days previously and an enema was administered in the ED with satisfactory results. He was discharged with laxatives and an indwelling catheter.

report.source_text: The following day after his third discharge he presented for the fourth and final time, with headache, neck stiffness, vomiting and dramatically reduced coordination in his lower limbs. On examination he was alert with no photophobia or confusion, and normal power and sensation in his upper limbs. However, power and coordination were reduced bilaterally in his lower limbs and reflexes were difficult to elicit. A broad-based, ataxic gait was observed. He was admitted and apixaban was stopped due to a clinical suspicion of haemorrhagic spinal pathology.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on apixaban presented to the ED with sudden onset mid-back pain following a long-haul flight. Initial ED evaluation (Day 1) included D-dimer testing (negative), stable vital signs, and no focal neurological findings; he was discharged with a diagnosis of mechanical back pain and analgesia. He returned on Day 2 with severe recurrent burning pain through the shoulder blades, new onset hypoxia on arterial blood gas, and stiff calves. CT aortogram was performed to rule out aortic dissection or PE (both excluded); reactive lymph nodes were noted and he was discharged on antibiotics for presumed infection. On Day 3, he presented with urinary retention (1300 mL on bladder scan); neurological examination at that time showed normal lower limb power and sensation with normal anal tone. Urinary retention was attributed to codeine-induced constipation; he was catheterized and discharged with laxatives. On Day 4, he presented with headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, and dramatically reduced coordination and power in his lower limbs bilaterally with an ataxic gait, while upper limb power and sensation remained normal and reflexes were difficult to elicit. Apixaban was stopped due to clinical suspicion of haemorrhagic spinal pathology. Urgent head CT showed a small possible subarachnoid haemorrhage. MRI of the spine revealed findings initially reported as thoracic syringomyelia in T1–T5 with extension in L4–S1, which was confirmed as spinal subdural haematoma. Repeat MRI performed 1 month after initial imaging demonstrated near complete resolution of the haematoma.
